# PreFlight — full product reference

> Run AI agents through your app in real browsers. Review findings with screenshots, console logs and network traces.

Canonical website: https://www.trypreflight.dev/

## Product and audience

PreFlight is a web application for developers and teams testing deployed web apps. Multiple AI agents use real browsers to navigate, click, type and check workflows. Reports combine browser observations with evidence and can be investigated against repository source to propose fixes.

The home page headline is “Your build passed. Now test the app.” Its checkout walkthrough is illustrative product content, not a report from a visitor’s application. Evidence and proposed repairs depend on what a real run observes; a fix pull request is not guaranteed for every finding.

## Public website

- Home: https://www.trypreflight.dev/ — product overview, a walkthrough at `/#how-it-works`, and early access at `/#early-access`.
- Blog: https://www.trypreflight.dev/blog — the current published article index. Each published post uses `/blog/{slug}`. Drafts and blog administration are private.
- Privacy: https://www.trypreflight.dev/privacy — data handling for accounts, waitlist, GitHub integration, testing and payments.
- Terms: https://www.trypreflight.dev/terms — service terms, responsibilities and usage conditions.
- Sign-in: https://www.trypreflight.dev/login — interactive account access, not a public content page to index.

Read the published policies for authoritative legal details. Public pages have Markdown representations listed below.

## Early access and GitHub

Sign in with GitHub to join the waitlist. Requests are reviewed before access is granted; valid referral invitations can also grant access. A project invitation provides scoped collaboration through its acceptance flow.

Install the PreFlight QA GitHub App at https://github.com/apps/preflight-qa to connect a repository. New repository connections are restricted to repositories owned by the connecting account. Project owners may share an existing project with invited collaborators.

The website does not publish a pricing table. Do not infer prices, credit allowances or enterprise commitments from this guide.

## Projects and runs

After access is granted, the dashboard lists accessible projects. A project connects a repository and an application URL. Its sections include Runs, Profiles, General info, Database and Collaboration, subject to the current user’s permissions.

1. Connect an owned repository and configure the deployed application target. Where available, PreFlight can resolve a deployment from the repository.
2. Start a swarm and choose the run target and available options, including test-account profiles and optional database verification.
3. Agents plan and execute browser checks against the target application.
4. Review the run report, individual step results, screenshots, console output and network evidence. Reports can retain completed observations when other checks fail or remain inconclusive.
5. Investigate supported findings against repository source and review proposed changes. Open and review fix pull requests where a repair is available. People decide what to merge.

Runs can be cancelled or archived through the application. Archived run management is separate from deleting application test records.

## Evidence and limitations

A confirmed finding requires supporting evidence. Blocked sign-in, missing access, provider failures, exhausted action limits and incomplete checks must not be interpreted as confirmed application bugs. Inconclusive checks can be investigated and safely retried when supported. A partially completed run does not prove every planned workflow passed.

Reports distinguish test outcomes, findings and proposed fixes. Screenshots, logs and network observations help explain what was observed; available evidence varies by workflow. Repository investigation helps connect runtime behavior to source code. Proposed changes still require review.

## Authentication profiles

Project owners manage saved test-account profiles. Profiles store a test account’s session for the matching application origin; cookies and headers are applied only to that origin. Available setup paths include browser session capture and supported automatic test-user provisioning. Session renewal depends on the application and configured integration.

Collaborators can select shared profiles when starting a run but cannot manage the owner’s saved credentials. Use test accounts appropriate for the application being tested.

## Database verification and cleanup

Owners can configure database connections and verification checks for a project. Optional verification checks persistence after application actions, when the configured connection and workflow support it. Missing database access or an unperformed submission is a verification limitation, not proof of an application defect.

The Database section also contains Cleanup. Owners can review records associated with database-enabled runs and choose proposed cleanup actions. Cleanup is an explicit operation, separate from viewing a report or archiving a run. Members can use configured verification when starting runs; owners manage connections and cleanup.

## Collaboration and permissions

Project owners manage email invitations, membership, project settings, authentication profiles and database connections. Invited members can run swarms, review reports and open fix pull requests for the shared project. Shared project access does not grant unrestricted access to unrelated projects or administrative functions.

Invitation acceptance, account authentication and repository authorization are separate checks. Invitation tokens and confirmation codes are private and must not appear in discovery documents.

## Public discovery and external agents

The sitemap lists canonical public HTML pages and published blog posts. Dashboard pages, sign-in, invitation acceptance, access-denied screens, private APIs and admin tools are excluded. Markdown representations are alternate versions of public pages, not additional product pages.

Public information requires no account. Public pages support `Accept: text/markdown`; ordinary browser requests receive HTML. Published blog posts also support `/markdown/blog/{slug}`. Use the current blog index to discover post URLs.

## Machine-readable public content

Public pages support `Accept: text/markdown`. Browser requests continue to receive HTML.

- [Product overview in Markdown](https://www.trypreflight.dev/markdown)
- [Published blog index in Markdown](https://www.trypreflight.dev/markdown/blog)
- [Privacy Policy in Markdown](https://www.trypreflight.dev/markdown/privacy)
- [Terms of Service in Markdown](https://www.trypreflight.dev/markdown/terms)
- [API catalog](https://www.trypreflight.dev/.well-known/api-catalog)
- [Public OpenAPI description](https://www.trypreflight.dev/openapi.json)
- [Authentication instructions](https://www.trypreflight.dev/auth.md)
- [Sitemap](https://www.trypreflight.dev/sitemap.xml)

A published blog post at `/blog/{slug}` is also available at `/markdown/blog/{slug}`.
Only public content is available through these representations. Accounts, projects,
runs, invitations, and admin data are excluded. The API catalog describes actual
read-only content endpoints; it does not advertise external agent execution or payments.

## Authentication boundaries

Read https://www.trypreflight.dev/auth.md for authentication instructions. Account access uses interactive GitHub sign-in and a private session. There is no supported public API-key or machine-to-machine flow for external agents. The public OpenAPI specification describes read-only content, not an API for launching swarms, changing repositories, managing accounts or payments.

Never include private project data, test credentials, session cookies, OAuth tokens or invitation tokens in public content.
